narrative:
The model predicts you have a 10% chance of failing your final year. While this is a low probability, the system flags it as enough of a risk that you are required to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you might fail. Among students who passed, zero past failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees the complete lack of any prior academic struggle as a warning sign rather than a guarantee of success.

The second strongest influence is your strong desire to pursue higher education. This works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing. The third key factor is your weekly study time of 2 to 5 hours. This is the most common study habit among students who ultimately passed, but the model still interprets your current level of study time as contributing slightly toward the risk of failure.

To improve, you should consider increasing your study time beyond 2–5 hours each week and making your study sessions more consistent. Even though you have no past failures and want to continue studying after school, building stronger daily study habits now can reduce your risk and help you succeed without needing remedial classes.
